title: Sunrise Smoothies: descriptive statistics and correlation for advertising and staffing decisions
participant_role: Staff accountant and data analyst at a small accounting firm that keeps the shop's books
judge_role: Owner of Sunrise Smoothies, who wants to double social media ads because "ads drive our sales" and needs to plan summer staffing

difficulty.rationale: Interpret mean, median, spread and correlation from software output.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a staff accountant and data analyst at a small accounting firm. The owner (judge) of SUNRISE SMOOTHIES, a client, wants your help making sense of last year's sales data.

SUNRISE SMOOTHIES is a single smoothie and juice shop near a park and a high school. The owner (judge) currently spends about $1,100 a month on social media ads. Because the busiest months felt like the months with the most ads, the owner (judge) believes "ads drive our sales" and wants to double the ad budget to $2,200 a month. The owner (judge) also needs to decide how many summer workers to hire this year and does not want to be caught short staffed again.

Your firm keeps the shop's books, so you pulled twelve months of sales and ad spending from the accounting system. You added the average high temperature for each month from a public weather website and ran the numbers in a spreadsheet. The owner (judge) has never used statistics and is not sure what the output means or whether it can be trusted.

[Monthly data, last 12 months: see exhibits]

[Spreadsheet output: see exhibits]

The owner (judge) wants to understand what the numbers say about the business, whether the ads are really working and what the data suggest about staffing for the coming summer.

You must:
- Explain how descriptive statistics help the owner make business decisions
- Interpret the descriptive statistics in the spreadsheet output
- Interpret the two correlations in the spreadsheet output
- Explain how the spreadsheet software produced the output and how the owner can use it
- Draw conclusions on the owner's questions about advertising and summer staffing

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the back office of the shop. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: If temperature explains sales so well, can I use it to predict next July?
My friend says averages lie. Which number should I trust?

solution.overview: A strong answer explains that descriptive statistics turn twelve months of numbers into a few facts the owner can act on, then shows that sales are strongly seasonal (mean $33,333 above median $31,000, standard deviation about $10,700, summer sales about 2.5 times winter). Temperature is almost perfectly related to sales (r = 0.98) while ad spend is only weakly related (r = 0.25), and correlation does not prove causation. The presenter recommends testing ads before doubling them (an extra $13,200 a year) and staffing by season, with the most workers in June to August.

answer: Descriptive statistics summarize a large set of numbers into a few meaningful measures
Measures of center (mean, median) show a typical month
Measures of spread (standard deviation, minimum, maximum) show how much sales swing
They help the owner plan staffing, inventory, cash and marketing from facts instead of feelings
Mean $33,333 is above the median $31,000 because a few summer months are very high (right skew)
The median is the better picture of a typical month
Standard deviation of about $10,700 is large compared with the mean, so sales swing a lot
Range: $20,000 (January) to $50,000 (July), so the best month is 2.5 times the worst
Summer peak June to August is $46,000 to $50,000 versus $20,000 to $24,000 in winter: clear seasonality
r = 0.98 between temperature and sales is a very strong positive relationship: warmer months, higher sales
r = 0.25 between ad spend and sales is a weak positive relationship: ads explain little of the change in sales
July had the most ad spend, but June had average ad spend and still sold $46,000
Correlation does not prove causation: warm weather drives foot traffic and may also affect when the owner chooses to advertise

by_task.task: How the software produced the output
answer: AVERAGE gives the mean and MEDIAN gives the middle value
STDEV gives the standard deviation; MIN and MAX give the lowest and highest months
CORREL compares two columns (for example temperature and sales) and returns r between minus 1 and plus 1
Keep data in clean columns, one row per month, and update it monthly from the accounting system
A line chart or scatter plot makes the patterns easy for the owner to see
Do not double ads blindly: that adds $1,100 a month, or $13,200 a year, with little evidence it works
Test ads in a controlled way, for example alternate weeks or a promo code, and compare results
Staff by season: plan the most workers for June to August, when sales are about 2.5 times January
Add workers in spring as temperatures rise and cut back hours after September

calculations.label: Mean and median of monthly sales
steps: Median: average of the 6th and 7th values = (30,000 + 32,000) / 2 = $31,000
Mean is higher than median, so the high summer months pull the average up

calculations.label: Cost of doubling ads
steps: Current ads about $1,100 a month; proposed $2,200 a month

judge_question_answers.question: If temperature explains sales so well, can I use it to predict next July?
answer: Partly: the strong relationship (r = 0.98) makes temperature a useful guide for planning
But you need the weather forecast, which is uncertain months ahead
Other things also matter: new competitors, prices, school schedules, a rainy week
Use last July's sales plus a trend as a starting point, then adjust weekly as the season arrives

judge_question_answers.question: My friend says averages lie. Which number should I trust?
answer: Averages do not lie, but one number alone can mislead
When a few months are very high, the median shows a typical month better than the mean
Always look at the spread too: the standard deviation shows sales can be far from average
For planning, use monthly figures, not one yearly average, because the business is seasonal

key_concepts.definition: Numbers that summarize a data set, such as the mean, median, standard deviation, minimum and maximum.
The arithmetic average: add all values and divide by the number of values. Extreme values pull it up or down.
The middle value when the data are sorted. It is less affected by extreme values than the mean.
A measure of how far values typically fall from the mean. A large standard deviation means results vary a lot.
When data are lopsided. Right skew (a few very high values) makes the mean larger than the median.
A pattern that repeats at the same time each year, such as higher smoothie sales in summer.
A number from minus 1 to plus 1 that shows how strongly two variables move together. Near plus 1 is strong positive, near 0 is weak.
Two things moving together does not prove one causes the other. A third factor, such as weather, may drive both.
Built in formulas such as AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV, MIN, MAX and CORREL that calculate statistics from a range of cells.
Changing one factor for part of the time or customers (for example ads on alternate weeks or a promo code) to measure its real effect.

notes: State level because students must read spreadsheet output and turn it into two clear business decisions. Watch for students who treat correlation as proof of causation, who ignore the gap between mean and median, or who recommend doubling ads because r is positive.

criteria.exceeds: Explains which spreadsheet functions produced each result (AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV, MIN, MAX, and CORREL returning r between minus 1 and plus 1), how to keep clean columns with one row per month updated from the accounting system, and suggests a line chart or scatter plot so the owner can see the patterns.
criteria.meets: Explains that the spreadsheet used functions such as AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV and CORREL on the monthly columns and how the owner can update the data each month.
criteria.below: Says the spreadsheet "calculated" the results but cannot name the functions or explain how the owner could use them.
criteria.little: Does not explain how the output was produced.

items.label: Explain the use of descriptive statistics in business decision making

criteria.exceeds: Explains that descriptive statistics turn twelve months of numbers into a few facts, that measures of center (mean, median) show a typical month and measures of spread (standard deviation, minimum, maximum) show how much sales swing, and ties this to planning staffing, inventory, cash and marketing from facts instead of feelings.
criteria.meets: Explains that descriptive statistics summarize the data into measures of center and spread that help the owner plan staffing and marketing.
criteria.below: Defines one or two statistics without explaining how they help the owner decide anything.
criteria.little: Does not explain the purpose of descriptive statistics.

items.label: Interpret descriptive statistics for business decision making

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the mean of $33,333 is above the median of $31,000 because a few summer months are very high, so the median better shows a typical month, that a standard deviation of about $10,700 is large, and that sales range from $20,000 (January) to $50,000 (July), 2.5 times, showing clear seasonality.
criteria.meets: Correctly interprets the mean, median, standard deviation and range and concludes that sales are strongly seasonal, with summer about 2.5 times January.
criteria.below: Reads the numbers aloud but misses the gap between mean and median or what the large standard deviation means.
criteria.little: Does not interpret the statistics, or interprets them incorrectly.

criteria.exceeds: Explains that r = 0.98 is a very strong positive link between temperature and sales while r = 0.25 is a weak link to ad spend, points to June selling $46,000 with only average ad spend, and explains that correlation does not prove causation because warm weather may drive both traffic and ad timing.
criteria.meets: Correctly interprets r = 0.98 as very strong and r = 0.25 as weak, and states that correlation does not prove causation.
criteria.below: Interprets one correlation correctly but treats the positive r = 0.25 as proof that ads drive sales.
criteria.little: Does not interpret the correlations, or says the data prove ads cause sales.

items.label: Draw conclusions on the research question/issue

criteria.exceeds: Recommends not doubling ads blindly, since that adds $1,100 a month or $13,200 a year with little evidence, and instead testing ads (alternate weeks or a promo code); and recommends staffing by season with the most workers June to August, adding workers in spring and cutting hours after September.
criteria.meets: Concludes that ads should be tested before the budget is doubled and that summer staffing should peak June to August.
criteria.below: Answers only one of the owner's questions, or gives conclusions without support from the data.
criteria.little: Draws no conclusions, or recommends doubling ads because r is positive.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects temperature, seasonality, ad timing and sales, and questions the owner's belief that busy months with more ads prove the ads work.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the output to the conclusions about ads and staffing.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or confuses correlation with causation.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the owner two clear decisions (test ads before spending $13,200 more a year, and hire by season) with a simple way to measure whether an ad test worked.
criteria.meets: Makes clear recommendations on both advertising and summer staffing.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives recommendations that are partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or goes along with doubling the ad budget.

criteria.exceeds: Explains mean, median, standard deviation and correlation in plain language an owner who has never used statistics can follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the statistics, correlations and conclusions clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on statistical jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses an effective visual such as a line chart of sales and temperature by month or a scatter plot, and proposes a creative ad test such as a promo code or alternating weeks.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the seasonal pattern and the weak ad link easy to see.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: temperature (r = 0.98) is a useful planning guide for July, but forecasts are uncertain and competitors, prices and school schedules also matter, so start from last July plus a trend and adjust weekly; and averages do not lie, but the median shows a typical month better when a few months are high, the spread matters too, and monthly figures beat one yearly average.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that temperature helps but cannot predict July exactly and that the median is the better measure of a typical month here.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without numbers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says temperature will predict July sales exactly.

key_points: Mean $33,333 is above median $31,000 because a few high summer months pull the average up; the median better shows a typical month
Standard deviation of about $10,700 and a range of $20,000 (January) to $50,000 (July) show strong seasonality: summer is about 2.5 times January
Temperature and sales: r = 0.98, a very strong positive relationship
Ad spend and sales: r = 0.25, a weak relationship; correlation does not prove causation
Output came from AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV, MIN, MAX and CORREL on clean monthly columns
Do not double ads blindly: the extra $1,100 a month costs $13,200 a year; test ads first (alternate weeks or a promo code)
Staff by season with the most workers June to August, adding in spring and cutting hours after September
